moments.title: Why the RBI is pushing Tata Sons to list: it starts with ₹2 lakh crore
moments.summary: The opening frames the whole story on one number — roughly ₹2 lakh crore of assets. Tata Sons has been private all these years, and it is the size of the balance sheet plus its stakes across the group that brings the RBI in.
moments.evidence: Why is the RBI pushing TataSans towards the listing? The answer starts with one number, rupees 2 lakh crore. That's roughly the size of TataSans assets.

moments.title: What listing would change: disclosure, and answering to public shareholders
moments.summary: The mechanism, in one line: once it lists, more about what the company does and earns becomes public, and it acquires public shareholders it has to answer to.
moments.evidence: Once TataSans list, more information about what TataSans does, earns will be made available to the public. And TataSans will have the public shareholders to answer to.

moments.title: Why an investor should care: today you cannot buy the parent, only the pieces
moments.summary: The part aimed at the viewer. Tata Sons sits at the top and owns pieces of TCS, Tata Motors and Tata Steel, plus unlisted businesses including Air India and Tata Electronics. Today you can only buy a listed Tata company; a listing would let people buy into the parent itself.
moments.evidence: TataSans sits at the top of the Tata Group and it owns pieces of many listed companies like TCS, Tata Motors or Tata Steel. If TataSans list, investors could get a chance to buy a piece of the mothership which not only owns these listed companies but some unlisted ones like Air India and Tata Electron.

moments.title: Tata Trusts opposes it — public shareholders versus philanthropy
moments.summary: The objection, and it is the most quotable part: Tata Trusts, which owns about 66%, argues that bringing in public shareholders could change how the group balances business against philanthropy. Noel Tata has proposed splitting Tata Sons into smaller entities instead.
moments.evidence: The Tata Trust which own about 66% of TataSans is against listing for this very reason. Their argument is bringing public shareholders into TataSans could change the way TataSans balances business with philanthropy. So Noel Tata, the chairman of the Tata Trust has proposed splitting TataSans into smaller entities.

moments.title: A boardroom question over a chairman reappointment — names unverified
moments.summary: The closing item raises a question about someone's role in the reappointment of the Tata Sons chairman, and about business links to his family. The automatic transcript garbles both surnames here, so the substance is recorded but no name from this passage should be quoted or published without listening back to the audio first.
moments.evidence: And there's another development inside the TataSans boardroom.
